title: GEESE
subtitle: The band from New York.
articleTitle: RUIDO PARA UNA CIUDAD QUE NO DUERME
author: Por Vera Ledesma
paragraphs: En un subsuelo de Brooklyn, mientras el tren retumba bajo el piso y una lámpara insiste en parpadear, Geese afina como si estuviera armando una máquina. Cada instrumento avanza en una dirección diferente, pero el choque termina formando una sola criatura: nerviosa, imprevisible y extrañamente precisa.
La banda creció entre salas de ensayo prestadas, cables enredados y conciertos donde la mitad del público todavía no sabía qué estaba escuchando. Esa incertidumbre se volvió parte de su lenguaje.

"Nos interesa el momento en que una canción casi se rompe", dice uno de sus integrantes en esta entrevista imaginaria. No habla de caos gratuito, sino de tensión: tocar lo suficientemente cerca del borde como para que cada decisión importe.

Nueva York aparece en su música sin necesidad de ser nombrada. Está en la urgencia, en las capas que compiten por espacio y en la sensación de que algo distinto puede ocurrir al doblar cualquier esquina.

Antes de irnos, vuelven a tocar el mismo fragmento. Esta vez dura menos de un minuto y suena completamente distinto. Quizás ahí esté la clave: para Geese, una canción no es un destino fijo, sino una pregunta que cambia cada vez que alguien intenta responderla.
note: Este reportaje es una pieza editorial ficticia creada para ARE WE THERE YET?

author: By Elías Grau
paragraphs: David Lynch rarely needed to create an entirely unfamiliar world in order to make a place feel strange. Most of the spaces in his films are immediately recognizable: hotel corridors, living rooms, theaters, highways, industrial buildings or apartments. However, there is usually something slightly wrong with them. The proportions seem unusual, the lighting does not reveal enough, a hallway extends farther than expected or a room appears disconnected from the building that supposedly contains it. Lynch takes spaces that we understand instinctively and removes some of the information that normally allows us to feel comfortable inside them.

This is closely related to what we now describe as a liminal space, a place that exists primarily as a transition between two others. A corridor connects rooms, a staircase connects floors, a motel exists between departure and arrival, and a highway is essentially a long space between two destinations. These places normally have little importance of their own because we are supposed to pass through them. Lynch does the opposite: he makes us remain there long enough for the transition itself to become the subject.

The Red Room in Twin Peaks is probably the clearest example. At first sight, it contains elements we already recognize: chairs, lamps, curtains and a floor. Yet none of these elements give us enough information to understand where the room actually is. There are no conventional walls, no visible windows and no obvious relationship between the interior and an exterior building. The red curtains divide the space without explaining what exists behind them, while the black-and-white floor exaggerates depth instead of helping us understand it. It resembles a room, but it does not behave like one.

This ambiguity is fundamental because architecture normally helps us understand our position. Even when we enter an unfamiliar building, doors, windows and corridors allow us to construct a mental map almost automatically. Lynch frequently interrupts this process. In his films, entering a room does not guarantee that we understand where we have arrived, and opening a door can create more uncertainty than the space that came before it. As a result, architecture stops functioning simply as a background and becomes part of the narrative itself.

A similar mechanism appears throughout Mulholland Drive. Los Angeles is presented as a recognizable city, but the characters repeatedly move through apartments, theaters, streets and houses that seem disconnected from one another. Club Silencio is especially important because it transforms the idea of a theater into something more ambiguous. A theater normally establishes a clear division between performance and reality: something happens on stage and an audience observes it. In Club Silencio, that distinction collapses. The performance openly reveals itself as an illusion, but the emotional response it produces remains real. The physical space therefore reflects one of Lynch's recurring ideas: knowing that something is artificial does not necessarily make its effect less powerful.

The highway in Lost Highway produces the same sensation through a completely different space. A road should represent movement and direction, but Lynch repeatedly shows it surrounded by darkness, with almost no visible landscape beyond the headlights. The result is movement without orientation. We know that the car is advancing, but the image gives us very little evidence of where it comes from or where it is going. The highway stops connecting two places and becomes a place in itself.

This is also why Lynch's work is often compared to dreams, although his spaces are rarely surreal in the conventional sense. A dream does not always invent impossible buildings; instead, it reorganizes familiar ones. Your childhood bedroom can suddenly connect to your university, or a hallway from one house can end inside another. While dreaming, these contradictions usually seem reasonable because each individual element remains recognizable. Lynch constructs spaces according to a similar logic. The objects make sense separately, but their relationship does not.

His earlier work already shows this interest. In Eraserhead, industrial architecture surrounds Henry Spencer with pipes, concrete, machinery and empty terrain. The city is never explained as a complete geographical place. Instead, we experience fragments of it: an apartment, a corridor, a factory-like landscape and rooms that seem isolated from a larger world. The environment becomes difficult to map, which reinforces the sensation that Henry is trapped inside something larger than himself without being able to understand its limits.

What makes these spaces particularly uncomfortable is not simply that they are empty. Contemporary internet culture has turned the idea of the “liminal space” into a recognizable aesthetic: abandoned shopping centers, empty schools at night, hotel corridors or fluorescent offices without people. Their strangeness usually comes from seeing a place designed for human activity without the humans who normally give it purpose. Lynch goes slightly further. His spaces rarely feel truly abandoned; instead, they often create the impression that someone has just left or that someone is about to arrive.

Therefore, the tension comes from expectation. A closed curtain matters because something could be behind it. An empty corridor becomes threatening because somebody could appear at the other end. A road surrounded by darkness implies a destination even when that destination remains invisible. Lynch does not need to show us the threat because the architecture already gives us enough information to imagine one.

This is perhaps one of the reasons his work remains so visually influential. Lynch understood that fear does not always require creating something completely unknown. Sometimes it is more effective to take something ordinary and make it slightly difficult to understand. A room does not have to contain a monster to become uncomfortable. It only has to stop behaving like the rooms we know.

In most architecture, a corridor is successful when we barely notice it. It takes us from one room to another and disappears from our memory once we arrive. Lynch understood the opposite possibility: what happens if we never quite reach the next room?

title:
THIS IS
NOT THE
END.
JUDAS
subtitle: Everybody loves you until you become somebody else.
author: By Sandy Harwol
paragraphs: Bob Dylan walks onstage in Manchester in 1966 wearing a dark suit that makes him look less like a folk singer and more like somebody who has arrived to collect a debt. His hair is enormous. He is twenty-four years old. This is important because twenty-four is very young to already have people complaining that you have betrayed everything you once represented.

The first half of the concert is easy enough. Dylan alone, acoustic guitar, harmonica, the version of him everybody had paid to see. It must have been comforting. There he was. Their Dylan. The protest singer. The mysterious skinny boy from Minnesota who somehow sounded as if he had been born seventy years old and on the side of a railway track.
Then there is an intermission.
This is where everything goes wrong.
He comes back with a band.
There are electric guitars now.
People hate the guitars.

I love this because an electric guitar today is such an ordinary object. You can buy one for a child. They hang in suburban bedrooms. You can plug one into a computer and make it sound like twenty other guitars. But in that room, in 1966, the guitar had become an ideological problem.
Imagine being angry at electricity.

Not really electricity, obviously. They were angry because electricity meant something. It meant Dylan had changed teams. Folk audiences had developed this strange relationship with authenticity where the instrument itself became part of the morality. Acoustic meant honest. Electric meant commercial. Acoustic meant Woody Guthrie. Electric meant screaming teenagers and Coca-Cola.
People always like authenticity until the authentic person decides they authentically want to do something else.

The tour had already been hostile. Audiences booed. People walked out. There were arguments in the crowd. Dylan kept doing it anyway, which is one of the best things you can do once people start demanding that you stop.
Then, before the final song in Manchester, somebody shouts:
“Judas!”
It is a wonderful insult.
It is completely insane.
Calling somebody Judas means they haven't merely disappointed you. They have betrayed something sacred. You need a Jesus in the story. You need disciples. You need a cause.
Apparently Bob Dylan playing an electric guitar had all three.

The funniest part is that whoever shouted it probably thought they were ruining the evening. Instead they accidentally made themselves immortal. We don't know that person's face the way we know Dylan's face. We don't buy posters of them. But their voice is trapped in the recording forever, like an insect in amber, yelling one very dramatic word at exactly the right historical moment.
Dylan hears it.
He answers: “I don't believe you. You're a liar.”
Then he turns toward the Hawks and tells them to play loud.
And they play Like a Rolling Stone.
This is almost too perfect, which is why I like that it actually happened.
If somebody wrote the scene for a movie you would probably tell them to make it less obvious.
The great betrayal ends with Like a Rolling Stone, a song about losing everything familiar and discovering that nobody is waiting to save you.
How does it feel?
Apparently very loud.

The audience believed Dylan belonged to them because they had understood him correctly once. This happens to artists all the time. People discover someone when their work expresses exactly what they need it to express, and then confuse recognition with ownership.
You saved me.
Therefore you are mine.
Please continue saving me in exactly the same way.
Forever.
It's a terrible contract.
Dylan's crime was not really becoming electric. His crime was making the transformation impossible to ignore. He could have changed gradually, politely, perhaps issued a little explanation.
Instead there was a drummer.
There was Robbie Robertson.
There were amplifiers.
There was volume.
The change had a costume.

I think audiences actually like artists changing when the new version arrives slowly enough that nobody has to admit they were wrong about the old one. David Bowie understood this and simply killed the previous character every few years. Much cleaner. If you become another person completely, people can collect both versions.
Dylan didn't give them that courtesy.
He was still Bob Dylan.
Same face.
Same songs.
Wrong guitar.
That must have been unbearable.

And now, of course, history has made the audience look ridiculous because history is unfair like that. Electric Dylan became Dylan. Blonde on Blonde came out. The music entered museums and documentaries and college courses. The act of betrayal became one of the most celebrated decisions in popular music.
This is the convenient thing about revolutions after they work.
Everybody likes them.
The photograph looks good.
The jacket becomes iconic.
The guitar goes behind glass.
Eventually even rebellion becomes merchandise.
I wonder what the man who shouted Judas thought ten years later.
Maybe he still hated it.
I hope so.
It would make the story better.
Because there is something slightly depressing about imagining him eventually buying Blonde on Blonde and admitting everybody else was right.
Maybe betrayal requires somebody who refuses to forgive you.
Otherwise it just becomes career development.
What interests me most about the recording now isn't really whether Dylan was right. Obviously he was right for himself, which is probably the only version that matters.
It's that you can hear a cultural change while it is still being rejected.

Most history arrives cleaned up. The important decisions appear inevitable because we already know what happened next. You see an old photograph of Dylan with an electric guitar and it looks completely natural.
Of course Bob Dylan played electric guitar.
But for a few seconds on that tape, it wasn't obvious at all.
It was offensive.
It was fake.
It was betrayal.
It was Judas.
Then the drums came in.
